title: 2100Q and 2100Qis User Manual
locator: Section 1, p. 3, specifications. Sections 6.3–6.4, pp. 10–12, calibration, sample handling and measurement.
summary: The guide distinguishes the 2100Q tungsten lamp and the 2100Qis LED. It explains how to calibrate with standards, orient the cell consistently and avoid contamination or bubbles that affect light scattering.
scope: Check the model suffix and record the meter's displayed unit. The 2100Q reports NTU and the 2100Qis reports FNU. Different optics can give different readings on the same natural sample.

title: Jar Testing Made Easy
publisher: California State Water Resources Control Board, Division of Drinking Water
locator: Jar Test Field Study, Measurements, pp. 1–2. Jar Test Procedures (1-Liter Jars) – Overview, p. 18.
summary: Schott describes a bench comparison of coagulants using source water from drinking-water plants. The procedure separates turbidity after settling from turbidity after filtration so the operator can compare two different treatment outcomes.
scope: The jar tester, mixing conditions, sampling stage and filtration arrangement must reflect the process under study. A portable meter measures the collected samples and supplies only the turbidity part of the experiment.
rights: Public agency document link and original summary.

title: Method 180.1: Determination of Turbidity by Nephelometry
locator: Sections 1–2, scope and principle. Sections 4 and 6.1–6.4, interferences and optical design. Sections 10–11, calibration and measurement.
summary: The procedure compares light scattered by a water sample with calibration standards. Its stated direct range is 0–40 NTU. It describes dilution for higher readings, and flags bubbles, settling particles and sample color as sources of bias.
scope: Applies to drinking, surface and saline water and wastes under its specified tungsten-lamp optics. The 2100Qis uses different optics. Its FNU results cannot be relabeled as EPA 180.1 NTU measurements.
rights: Federal agency publication link and original summary.

title: Guidelines and Procedures for Computing Time-Series Suspended-Sediment Concentrations and Loads from In-Stream Turbidity-Sensor and Streamflow Data
version: Rasmussen et al., Techniques and Methods 3–C4, revised 2011. DOI 10.3133/tm3C4
locator: Model-Calibration Data Set, pp. 6–12. Regression Model Development, pp. 12–19. Sampling Plan and Changes to Turbidity Sensor Model or Type, pp. 23–25.
summary: Pair turbidity readings with independently measured suspended sediment concentrations. The authors describe how to assess the calibration data, inspect model residuals and report prediction intervals before estimating sediment from optical readings.
scope: The published time-series method uses an in-stream sensor and streamflow. For a grab-sample study, build and check a new relationship with the local meter, sediment and sampling conditions. Estimating a river load also requires representative flow and concentration records.
rights: Federal agency publication link and original summary.

title: Evaluation of Annona diversifolia Seed Extract as A Natural Coagulant for Water Treatment
locator: Section 2.2.2 names the Hach 2100Q and describes sampling the supernatant. Section 3.2, Figures 3–4, and Table 5 compare turbidity reduction.
summary: The researchers measured turbidity before and after bench jar tests on a kaolin suspension and on river water. They compared pH and coagulant dose, finding that the effects on clarity depended on the coagulant and water matrix.
scope: The paper explicitly names the 2100Q in the kaolin procedure. Compare the matrices and the time allowed for settling before interpreting removal percentages. These experiments do not establish drinking-water safety.
rights: Open-access publisher article and original summary.

title: Application of a Polymer in Drinking Water Treatment: A Case Study
publisher: ICCESD 2020, Khulna University of Engineering & Technology
locator: Section 3.2, Experimental setup, p. 4. Section 4.1 and Table 2 show the dose series and settled-water measurements.
summary: The team used a Hach 2100Qis to compare settled river water after jar tests with alum, polymer or both. Table 2 shows that increasing the polymer dose did not produce a steady increase in turbidity removal.
scope: A conference study of one water source and one polymer. The paper labels readings NTU despite naming an infrared meter. Preserve its original labels when citing the study and record the local meter's actual unit.
rights: Conference proceedings link and original summary.

title: Effects of suspended sediment concentration and grain size on three optical turbidity sensors
version: Merten, Capel and Minella, volume 14, pp. 1235–1241. DOI 10.1007/s11368-013-0813-0
locator: Public abstract, Materials and methods and Results and discussion. Compare the fixed-concentration mixtures with different proportions of sand and fines.
summary: At a fixed sediment concentration of 1,000 mg/L, increasing the sand fraction reduced the optical signal. The three sensors were much more sensitive to fine material than to medium sand, illustrating why equal sediment masses can give different turbidity readings.
scope: This is an experiment on grain size and detector geometry. Its reported sensitivity ratios belong to the sensors and sediments tested. Pair local samples with a mass measurement before estimating a concentration.
rights: Publisher's public abstract and original summary. Full text may require institutional access.

title: Turbidity and suspended sediment relationship based on sediment composition and particle size distribution
version: Kim et al., volume 15, article 16286. DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-00435-2
locator: Figure 3d and equations 1–3 compare size fractions. Figure 5 shows the fraction-based models. Discussion describes three days of field validation.
summary: In a circulating flume, the team fitted separate sediment–turbidity regressions for sieved material. The finest fraction gave an R² of 0.99 and the coarsest tested fraction gave 0.86. This provides a practical comparison for testing whether one calibration covers different particle mixtures.
scope: The validation included only three field days in a South Korean watershed. The reported regressions are specific to those measurements. Refit a local relationship for a different meter, grain distribution or watershed.
rights: Open-access publisher article and original summary.
